summary: Diabetes is a long-term condition in which blood sugar stays too high because the body does not make enough insulin or cannot use it well. Type 1 usually starts early and needs insulin; type 2 is more common in adults and is linked to weight, activity and family history. Gestational diabetes can appear during pregnancy.
symptoms: Many people with type 2 diabetes have no symptoms at first
causes: Type 1: the immune system damages insulin-producing cells.
Type 2: reduced insulin action combined with insufficient insulin over time.
risk_factors: Age above 30 to 35 (earlier screening is advised for many Indians at risk)
High blood pressure or abnormal cholesterol
History of gestational diabetes or PCOS

tests.name: Fasting plasma glucose
tests.purpose: Measures blood sugar after an overnight fast.

preparation.other: Preparation can differ between labs and between patients; follow the instructions of your doctor or lab.

tests.exceptions: Not suitable if the person is unwell or has been fasting for much longer; the doctor decides.

tests.name: HbA1c
tests.purpose: Shows average blood sugar over about 3 months.
tests.exceptions: Can be unreliable with anaemia, thalassaemia/haemoglobin variants, recent blood loss or transfusion, and in pregnancy; the doctor may choose a glucose test instead.

tests.name: Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
tests.purpose: Measures how the body handles a glucose drink; used for specific situations such as pregnancy screening.

preparation.fasting: Usually an overnight fast, as instructed by the lab or doctor.
preparation.other: Follow the lab's instructions about diet and rest before the test.

tests.exceptions: The glucose amount, timing and fasting rules differ in pregnancy; follow the antenatal doctor's protocol.

tests.name: Random plasma glucose
tests.purpose: A quick check when symptoms of high sugar are present.

tests.name: Kidney function, urine albumin and lipid profile
tests.purpose: Checks for complications and heart risk once diabetes is diagnosed.

preparation.fasting: Depends: a fasting sample is needed only for some lipid tests, the lab or doctor will tell you.

tests.exceptions: Not every patient needs every test at every visit.

prevention: Choose whole grains, pulses, vegetables and fruit; limit sugary drinks, sweets and refined foods
lifestyle: Take medicines or insulin only as prescribed; never stop or change them on your own
Check feet daily and wear comfortable footwear
Have regular eye, kidney and cholesterol checks as advised
red_flags: Vomiting, abdominal pain, fast breathing or fruity-smelling breath (possible diabetic ketoacidosis)
Sweating, shaking and sudden weakness in a person on diabetes medicine (possible very low sugar)
A foot wound that looks infected or is not healing
when_to_consult: Persistent thirst, frequent urination, weight loss or blurred vision
Adults with risk factors should ask a doctor about screening, even without symptoms
special_populations: Children and teenagers with these symptoms should see a doctor quickly (type 1 can progress fast)
Pregnancy: screening for gestational diabetes is done by the antenatal doctor with a specific protocol
Older adults may have fewer classic symptoms

faqs.q: Do I always need to fast for a diabetes test?
faqs.a: No. HbA1c and random glucose do not need fasting. Fasting glucose and some OGTT protocols do. Follow your doctor or lab.

faqs.q: Does one high reading confirm diabetes?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Doctors interpret results with symptoms and may repeat the test.

summary: The thyroid is a small gland in the neck that controls body metabolism. If it makes too little hormone (hypothyroidism) or too much (hyperthyroidism), many body systems are affected. A swelling in the neck (goitre) can occur in either case or with iodine deficiency.
symptoms: Hypothyroid pattern: tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold, dry skin, constipation, hair fall, low mood, heavy or irregular periods
Hyperthyroid pattern: weight loss, feeling hot, fast heartbeat, tremor, anxiety, sweating, loose motions
Swelling in the front of the neck
causes: Thyroid nodules, inflammation, or past thyroid surgery/treatment
risk_factors: Female sex and age above 30 to 35

tests.name: TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone)
tests.purpose: First-line test to see whether the thyroid is under- or overactive.

preparation.other: Same-time-of-day sampling helps compare repeated results. Tell the lab about thyroid medicine, biotin or other supplements.

tests.exceptions: Biotin supplements can disturb some lab results; the doctor may ask you to pause them for a few days before testing. Do not stop any prescribed medicine on your own.

tests.name: Free T4 (and sometimes Free T3)
tests.purpose: Confirms the type and degree of thyroid problem when TSH is abnormal.

preparation.other: Preparation can differ between labs and between patients; follow the instructions of your doctor or lab.

tests.name: Thyroid ultrasound
tests.purpose: Looks at neck swelling or nodules.

preparation.other: Usually no special preparation; follow the centre's instructions.

tests.exceptions: Ordered only when the doctor suspects a swelling or nodule.

prevention: Use iodised salt in normal amounts (WHO advises less than 5 g salt per day overall)
Do not take iodine or thyroid supplements without medical advice
lifestyle: If a thyroid medicine is prescribed, take it exactly as advised and keep follow-up tests
Do not change or stop the dose on your own
red_flags: Very fast or irregular heartbeat with chest pain or breathlessness
Neck swelling with difficulty breathing or swallowing
Extreme sleepiness, confusion, very slow heartbeat or feeling extremely cold
High fever, agitation and confusion in a person with known thyroid illness
when_to_consult: Persistent tiredness with weight change, hair fall, temperature intolerance or menstrual change
Any swelling or lump in the neck
special_populations: Pregnancy: thyroid levels are interpreted with pregnancy-specific ranges; consult the antenatal doctor early
Newborns and children: persistent tiredness, poor growth or neck swelling need a paediatrician
Older adults may have fewer typical symptoms

faqs.q: Do I need to fast for a thyroid test?
faqs.a: Usually not for TSH, but follow your doctor's or lab's instructions, especially about medicines and supplements like biotin.

faqs.q: Is weight gain always because of thyroid?
faqs.a: No. Many other causes exist; a doctor decides whether a thyroid test is needed.
